claim: fMRI data from 414 children and adolescents (5–19 years) were analyzed as they watched a narrative movie
source: Here, we analyzed fMRI data from 414 children and adolescents (5–19 years) as they watched a narrative movie.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and describes the dataset used in the study

claim: Age-related changes in inter-subject correlation (ISC) occur in sensory and medial parietal regions
source: In addition to changes in the degree of inter-subject correlation (ISC) with age in sensory and medial parietal regions
evidence: This finding is reported in the abstract and supported by data presented in Figure 1

claim: Age-related shifts in brain responses occur across the majority of the neocortex
source: we used a novel measure (between-group ISC) to reveal age-related shifts in the responses across the majority of the neocortex.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the between-group ISC analysis shown in Figure 2

claim: Brain responses become more discretized into stable and coherent events over the course of development
source: Over the course of development, brain responses became more discretized into stable and coherent events
evidence: This finding is reported in the abstract and supported by HMM analysis shown in Figures 4 and 5

claim: Brain responses shift earlier in time to anticipate upcoming perceived event transitions with age
source: Over the course of development, brain responses became more discretized into stable and coherent events and shifted earlier in time to anticipate upcoming perceived event transitions, measured behaviorally in an age-matched sample.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by timing analysis shown in Figure 6

claim: Hippocampal responses to event boundaries decrease with age
source: However, hippocampal responses to event boundaries actually decreased with age
evidence: This finding is reported in the abstract and supported by data shown in Figure 7

claim: There is a shifting division of labor between episodic encoding processes and schematic event representations between ages 5 and 19
source: suggesting a shifting division of labor between episodic encoding processes and schematic event representations between the ages of 5 and 19.
evidence: This interpretation is stated in the abstract based on the pattern of cortical and hippocampal findings

claim: The ability to perceive and remember the world changes radically throughout the first twenty years of life
source: The ability to perceive and remember the world changes radically throughout the first twenty years of life (Aslin and Smith, 1988; Schneider and Pressley, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research

claim: Older children and adolescents are better able to understand and interpret the world around them
source: Older children and adolescents are better able to understand and interpret the world around them, and anticipate upcoming situations (Carpendale and Lewis, 2006; Casillas and Frank, 2017; Richardson and Saxe, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research

claim: Much of the increase in ability can be attributed to greater familiarity with events that children are likely to encounter
source: Much of this increase in ability can be attributed to greater familiarity with the events that they are likely to encounter (Schneider and Pressley, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research

claim: Children have better memory for situations that they have expertise in
source: For instance, children have better memory for situations that they have expertise in (e.g. Chess; Chi, 1978).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research on chess expertise

claim: Children normally acquire and organize novel information about their world over the course of weeks, if not years
source: Children, however, normally acquire and organize novel information about their world over the course of weeks, if not years (Nelson, 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research

claim: Naturalistic narrative stimuli provide a tool for probing complex, real-world knowledge that children have acquired across repeated experiences
source: Naturalistic narrative stimuli provide a tool for probing this complex, real-world knowledge that children have acquired across repeated experiences and can deploy automatically (Cantlon and Li, 2013; Lerner et al., 2019; Petroni et al., 2018; Moraczewski et al., 2018; Moraczewski et al., 2020; Richardson et al., 2019; Richardson and Saxe, 2020; Vanderwal et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research

claim: The study utilized fMRI data acquired while children and adolescents between ages 5 and 19 watched a short narrative cartoon
source: We utilized functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data acquired while children and adolescents between the ages of 5 and 19 watched a short narrative cartoon that contained both social and emotional content (Alexander et al., 2017; Petroni et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the dataset and methods used in the study

claim: Children respond similarly to social cues in cartoons and live action videos
source: Although cartoons do not physically replicate the characteristics of everyday perception, there is evidence to suggest that children respond similarly to the social cues in cartoons and live action videos (Han et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research

claim: Inter-subject correlation (ISC) measures the similarity of brain responses in a brain region across movie viewers
source: A model-free approach to assess brain responses to this kind of stimuli is inter-subject correlation (ISC), which measures the similarity of brain responses in a brain region across movie viewers (Cantlon and Li, 2013; Lerner et al., 2019; Petroni et al., 2018; Moraczewski et al., 2018; Moraczewski et al., 2020).
evidence: This defines the ISC method and is supported by citations

claim: ISC within an age group has generally been found to increase with age
source: ISC within an age group has generally been found to increase with age, possibly due to more mature engagement with the content, greater shared knowledge about the world, or more exposure to widely used cinematic conventions (Cantlon and Li, 2013; Lerner et al., 2019; Moraczewski et al., 2018; Moraczewski et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research

claim: ISC increases with age in low level sensory regions such as the auditory cortex
source: We found (Figure 1) that ISC increases with age in low level sensory regions such as the auditory cortex
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1

claim: ISC decreases with age in some higher level association regions such as the retrosplenial cortex (RSC) portion of the PMC
source: and decreases with age in some higher level association regions such as the retrosplenial cortex (RSC) portion of the PMC.
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1

claim: There was no relationship between framewise displacement and ISC in parcels where ISC increased with age
source: There was no relationship between framewise displacement and ISC in any of the parcels where ISC increased with age, indicating that motion did not drive the result in these parcels (all q's>0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the analysis controlling for motion artifacts

claim: Eighty-one of the 100 parcels tested show significant age-specific response timecourses
source: Eighty-one of the 100 (Schaefer et al., 2018) parcels tested show significant age-specific response timecourses including default mode regions, such as the temporoparietal junction (TPJ) and PMC (Raichle et al., 2001), and language and concept sensitive regions, such as the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) and inferior temporal cortices, and orbitofrontal cortex (Binder and Desai, 2011; Ralph et al., 2017; Figure 2c).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2c

claim: There are small but significant differences in the timing of event boundaries marked by adults and children
source: There are small but significant differences in the timing of the event boundaries marked by adults and children (ISCb = 0.97, p=0.009).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from behavioral data analysis

claim: The timing of event boundaries was slightly but significantly different between the younger half and older half of the children
source: The timing of event boundaries was also slightly, but significantly different between the younger half and older half of the children (ISCb = 0.96, p=0.01, Figure 3).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from behavioral data shown in Figure 3

claim: In adults, movie responses are characterized by rapid transitions between stable periods of brain activity, corresponding to meaningful events in the narrative
source: In adults, movie responses are often characterized by rapid transitions between stable periods of brain activity, corresponding to meaningful events in the narrative (Baldassano et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research

claim: The HMM was able to identify event structure in 70 out of 100 parcels in at least one of the groups (Youngest and/or Oldest)
source: Fitting the HMM separately to the Youngest and Oldest groups, we found that the HMM was able to identify event structure in at least one of the groups (Youngest and/or Oldest) for 70 out of our 100 parcels (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: The optimal timescale was highly correlated between the Youngest and Oldest ages (r=0.78)
source: In these 71 parcels, we found that the optimal timescale (optimal number of events) was highly correlated between the Youngest and Oldest ages (r=0.78, RMS difference between groups = 12.3 s)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the HMM analysis

claim: Event timescales increase from sensory regions to higher level association regions
source: showing increasing timescales from sensory regions to higher level association regions (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2

claim: The timescale hierarchy is present even in the Youngest (5–8 years) age group
source: This replicates previous research showing increasing event timescales across the cortical hierarchy (Baldassano et al., 2020; Geerligs et al., 2021; Hasson et al., 2015), and shows that this timescale hierarchy is present even in our Youngest (5–8 years) age group.
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by data analysis

claim: The event boundaries from the HMM correspond to boundaries subjectively placed by human raters in association regions
source: As expected based on previous research in adults, the event boundaries from this model correspond to the boundaries subjectively placed by human raters in association regions, such as PMC, TPJ, and precuneus (Figure 5—figure supplement 3; Baldassano et al., 2020).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3

claim: The neural activity of the Oldest group can be better represented by an event model in most of the parcels that significantly differ with age
source: As hypothesized, the neural activity of the Oldest group can be better represented by an event model in most of the parcels that significantly differ with age.
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 5

claim: Regions with better event model fits in older subjects include sensory areas such as auditory and visual cortex, as well as left parietal operculum and dlPFC
source: These regions include sensory areas, such as the auditory and visual cortex, as well as the left parietal operculum and dlPFC (Figure 5).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5

claim: In sensory regions, the largest change in event model-fit occurs between children 5–8 years and those 8–11 years
source: In sensory regions, the largest change in event model-fit occurs between children 5–8 years and those 8–11 years (Figure 5, side panels).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5 side panels

claim: The left parietal operculum increases in model-fit through approximately age 13
source: The left parietal operculum increases in model-fit through approximately age 13.
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 5

claim: The HMM exhibits better model fits in the PMC for the Youngest group than the Oldest group
source: Surprisingly, the HMM exhibits better model fits in the PMC, including both the posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) and RSC, for the Youngest group than the Oldest group.
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 5

claim: Event boundaries occur earlier in time with age in sensory regions including auditory and visual cortex
source: This hypothesis was borne out in sensory regions including auditory and visual cortex, as well as left lateralized associative regions including the left precuneus and left dlPFC (Figure 6a).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6a

claim: Sensory regions are predictive at shorter time scales, consistent with their quicker processing speed
source: Sensory regions are predictive at shorter time scales, consistent with their quicker processing speed (Baldassano et al., 2020; Hasson et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research and data from Figure 6

claim: Higher level association regions anticipate upcoming events on average up to tens of seconds into the future
source: while the higher level association regions anticipate upcoming events on average up to tens of seconds into the future.
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 6

claim: Anticipation increases rapidly across ages 5–11 in the left dlPFC and left precuneus
source: This anticipation increases rapidly across ages 5–11 in the left dlPFC and left precuneus, with a more variable trajectory in left postcentral sulcus (side panels).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 6 side panels

claim: In the right ventral temporal cortex, the Youngest children anticipate upcoming events slightly sooner, and anticipation decreases almost linearly with age
source: However, as was seen for model-fit, this trend reverses in the right ventral temporal cortex where the Youngest children anticipate upcoming events slightly sooner, and anticipation decreases almost linearly with age.
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 6

claim: The Oldest group generally anticipates event shifts, while the Youngest ages generally lag behind them
source: Across the cortex we find that the Oldest ages generally anticipate event shifts, while the Youngest ages lag behind them to some degree (Figure 6b).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6b

claim: There is a robust response to event boundaries in all ages in the hippocampus
source: We found a robust response to event boundaries in all ages (all p's<0.0001 for each age group's response at time 0, see Figure 7a, right side).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7a

claim: The hippocampal response to event boundaries decreases with age between 5 and 19 years old (r=−0.16, p=1 × 10–3, N=414)
source: This response decreases with age between 5 and 19 years old (r=0.–16, p=1 × 10–3, N=414; Figure 7a).
evidence: This is a statistical finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 7a

claim: There is a significant decrease in the anterior hippocampal (aHPC) response to event boundaries with age (r=−0.18, p=2 × 10–4)
source: We found that there is a significant decrease in the anterior hippocampal (aHPC) response to event boundaries with age (r=−0.18, p=2 × 10–4, Figure 7b).
evidence: This is a statistical finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 7b

claim: There was no significant decrease in the posterior HPC (pHPC) response to event boundaries with age (r=−0.09, p=0.06)
source: We did not find a significant decrease in the posterior HPC (pHPC; r=−0.09, p=0.06, Figure 7c)
evidence: This is a statistical finding stated in the text and shown in Figure 7c

claim: There was no significant interaction between HPC subregions in the age-related change in boundary response (p=0.7)
source: nor a significant interaction between HPC subregions (p=0.7).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the analysis

claim: The change in boundary-related response was not explained by anatomical volume changes in any hippocampal region
source: In none of these regions was the change in boundary-related response explained by anatomical volume changes (see Methods).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by analysis described in Methods

claim: Older ages exhibit more across-subject synchrony in auditory cortex
source: Older ages exhibit more across-subject synchrony in auditory cortex (Figure 1), consistent with prior work showing developmental increases in ISC evoked by other similarly highly produced animated movies (Moraczewski et al., 2018).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text, shown in Figure 1, and supported by citation

claim: Theory of mind regions including TPJ develop immensely in the age range studied
source: Theory of mind regions responsible for representing the mental states of others (Gallagher et al., 2000; Saxe and Kanwisher, 2003), including TPJ (Samson et al., 2004), develop immensely in the age range studied (Sebastian et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research

claim: Very large age-related changes were found in the functional responses of TPJ
source: We found very large age-related changes in the functional responses of TPJ (Figure 2).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2

claim: In the right posterior-superior temporal sulcus and left postcentral sulcus, neural representations in 16–19 year-olds can be as far as 20 s ahead of those for 5–8 year-olds
source: In the right posterior-superior temporal sulcus (part of TPJ as defined by Dufour et al., 2013) and in the TPJ-adjacent left postcentral sulcus, we found that neural representations in 16–19 year-olds can be as far as 20 s ahead of those for 5–8 year-olds on the first viewing of a movie clip.
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 6

claim: Age-related shifts were found in dlPFC
source: We also found age-related shifts in dlPFC (Figure 2) and increasing anticipation from ages 5–11 (Figure 6).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and shown in Figures 2 and 6

claim: The dlPFC, inferior temporal cortex, and orbitofrontal cortex are part of a network responsible for processing conceptual knowledge about the world
source: This region, along with other regions showing age-related shifts such as the inferior temporal cortex and orbitofrontal cortex, are a part of a network responsible for processing conceptual knowledge about the world (Binder et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research

claim: The dlPFC is critical for working memory
source: The dlPFC is also critical for working memory, or the ability to keep recently learned information readily accessible (Curtis and D'Esposito, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research

claim: The dlPFC exhibits an improvement in event structure with age
source: The dlPFC exhibits an improvement in event structure with age (Figure 5)
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5

claim: In the PMC, event model fits worsened with age
source: In the PMC event model fits worsened with age (Figure 5)
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5

claim: In the RSC portion of PMC, reliability decreased with age
source: and in the more posterior RSC portion, reliability also decreased with age (Figure 1).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1

claim: PMC has significantly more activity in response to movies when the narrative topic is new than when it is a continuation of themes from the previous clip
source: Keidel et al., 2018 found that the PMC (RSC) had significantly more activity in response to movies when the narrative topic was new than when it was a continuation of themes from the previous clip.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research

claim: RSC is responsible for processing visual scenes and is fully developed by age 7
source: RSC is also known to be responsible for processing visual scenes and is fully developed by age 7 (Epstein and Baker, 2019; Meissner et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research

claim: PMC has an intrinsically long timescale for information processing, one that emerges in infancy
source: PMC has an intrinsically long timescale for information processing, one that emerges in infancy, which may thus support strong event models in children as young as five (Hasson et al., 2015; Stephens et al., 2013; Yates et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research

claim: Age-related shifts in the pattern of narrative representation were found bilaterally in PMC
source: However, we did find both age-related shifts in the pattern by which the narrative was represented bilaterally (Figure 2) and increased anticipation in the left PMC (Figure 6).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and shown in Figures 2 and 6

claim: Small but significant changes in the timecourse of narrative processing were found in the medial prefrontal cortex
source: We found small, but significant changes in the timecourse of narrative processing in the medial prefrontal cortex (Figure 2).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2

claim: The medial prefrontal cortex has been implicated in tracking schematic knowledge during movie-watching
source: This region has been previously implicated in tracking schematic knowledge during movie-watching (Baldassano et al., 2018; van Kesteren et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research

claim: The HPC reliably responds to the boundaries between events
source: The HPC was found to reliably respond to the boundaries between events (Figure 7).
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7

claim: The HPC tracks event changes in adults
source: This result extends evidence that the HPC tracks event changes in adults to children as young as five (Ben-Yakov and Henson, 2018; Baldassano et al., 2020; Reagh et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research

claim: Previous research in older adults found a decrease in the HPC response to event boundaries
source: Interestingly, previous research in older adults also found a decrease in the HPC response to event boundaries (Reagh et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research

claim: In previous research on older adults, the decrease with age was seen in the pHPC
source: However, in this previous research the decrease with age was seen in the pHPC (Reagh et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research

claim: The optimal event timescales in all regions with high model fits were similar between the Youngest and Oldest groups
source: Jointly fitting an HMM across children of different ages was sensible because we found that the optimal event timescales in all regions with high model fits were similar between the Youngest and Oldest groups.
evidence: This finding is stated in the text and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 2

claim: Infants under one year of age segment ongoing narratives into far fewer events than adults
source: This was not a foregone conclusion, because infants under one year of age segment ongoing narratives into far fewer events than adults (Yates et al., 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research

claim: Children develop enough narrative comprehension to segment the story in an adult-like manner by age five
source: However, at least neurally, children therefore develop enough narrative comprehension to segment the story in an adult-like manner by age five.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that timescales were similar between youngest and oldest groups

claim: The study analyzed fMRI data from 414 children and adolescents
source: Four hundred and twenty six subjects remained after these eliminations. To allow for a sufficient number of subjects (N=40) in each age group spanning 2.76 years, with an equivalent ratio of males to females in each age group, subjects older than 19 were not used in further analyses (N=11).
evidence: This describes the final sample size used in the study

claim: The data was downloaded from the Child Mind Institute's Health Brain Network (HBN) project
source: The data in these analyses was downloaded from the Child Mind Institute's Health Brain Network (HBN) project (Alexander et al., 2017) when 1758 MRI datasets were available (data release 6).
evidence: This describes the source of the data

claim: The goal of the HBN project was to collect data from subjects with heterogeneous developmental psychopathologies
source: The goal of the HBN project was to collect data from subjects with heterogeneous developmental psychopathologies.
evidence: This describes the nature of the dataset

claim: MRI data were collected at both the HBN Rutgers University Brain Imaging Center site on a Siemens Trio Tim 3T scanner and the HBN CitiGroup Cornell Brain Imaging Center site on a Siemens Prisma 3T scanner
source: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) data used in this study were collected at both the HBN Rutgers University Brain Imaging Center site on a Siemens Trio Tim 3T scanner and the HBN CitiGroup Cornell Brain Imaging Center site on a Siemens Prisma 3T scanner.
evidence: This describes the data acquisition sites and equipment

claim: fMRI data were collected while participants viewed a 10 min clip from the movie Despicable Me
source: fMRI data were collected while participants viewed a 10 min clip from the movie Despicable Me (01:02:09–01:12:09; presentation details available at http://fcon_1000.projects.nitrc.org/indi/cmi_healthy_brain_network/MRI%20Protocol.html).
evidence: This describes the stimulus used in the study

claim: A separate group of 21 adult raters watched the clip and recorded event boundaries
source: To obtain the timing of event boundaries, a separate group of 21 adult raters (6 males) watched the clip and were given the following instructions: "The movie clip can be divided into meaningful segments. Record the times (in seconds) denoting when you feel like a meaningful segment has ended. Pause the clip at the end of the segment, write down the time in the attached spreadsheet, and provide a short, descriptive title. Try to do this when you watch the clip for the first time."
evidence: This describes the behavioral data collection procedure

claim: On average, raters found 14.4+/-6.5 events in the movie (minimum = 4, maximum = 30)
source: On average, raters found 14.4+/-6.5 events in the movie (minimum = 4, maximum = 30).
evidence: This is a statistical summary of the behavioral data

claim: The volume of the entire hippocampus and aHPC correlated with subject age (entire HPC: r=–0.1, p=0.03, aHPC: r=–0.1, p=0.03)
source: The volume of the entire hippocampus and aHPC correlated with subject age (entire HPC: r=–0.1, p=0.03, aHPC: r=–0.1, p=0.03)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the anatomical analysis

claim: The volume of the pHPC did not correlate with age (r=–0.05, p=0.3)
source: while the volume of the pHPC did not (r=–0.05, p=0.3).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the anatomical analysis

claim: In none of the hippocampal regions was the age-matched event boundary response significantly correlated with the change in volume
source: However, in none of the regions was the age-matched event boundary response significantly correlated with the change in volume (entire HPC, r=0.01, p=0.9, aHPC, r=–0.01, p=0.9, pHPC, r=–0.03, p=0.6).
evidence: This is a statistical finding showing that volume changes do not explain functional changes

claim: Brain responses to a narrative movie become more synchronized across children as they age in some regions but change their dynamics and timing to become more adult-like across most of the cortex
source: Our results reveal that brain responses to a narrative movie do not simply become more synchronized across children as they age, but in fact change their dynamics and timing to become more adult-like.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the ISC and ISCb findings

claim: Brain activity patterns in many regions become more cleanly structured into discrete, consistent events with age
source: Brain activity patterns in many regions become more cleanly structured into discrete, consistent events, and the timing of these events shifts to anticipate upcoming content in the movie.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the HMM findings

claim: Hippocampal responses to event boundaries are present in children as young as 5 years old
source: We also found that hippocampal responses to event boundaries are present in children as young as 5 years old
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the discussion

claim: Event-boundary responses in the hippocampus are larger in children than in adolescents
source: and that these event-boundary responses are in fact larger in children than in adolescents.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the discussion based on Figure 7
